paper_title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Looped transformers (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Saunshi et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2026) apply the same layers over multiple loop steps, effectively reusing the same parameters across multiple iterations. Built on this parameter-efficient architecture, Ouro-1.4B Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers performs on par with non-looped models several times its size (Zhu et al., 2025). This parameter efficiency, however, does not extend to the key-value (KV) cache. Although the loop steps share their weights, each loop step stores its own keys and values, so the KV cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps. As Figure 1a shows, Ouro-1.4B requires six times the per-token KV cache of Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and the models KV cache exceeds its weights in memory even at moderate context lengths. This limits the batch size and context length at which the looped models can be served, making KV cache compression promising way to improve their efficiency. Among various KV cache compression methods, quantization compresses the KV cache by storing each key and value at lower precision, without discarding any tokens. It has been widely studied for standard LLMs, with both scalar (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024) and vector quantization (Zhang et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2026b; Son et al., 2026). These methods can also be applied to looped models, but they do not exploit the redundancy of the cache across loop steps, and below one bit per element they lose much of their accuracy (Figure 1b). We find that the keys and values of layer are strongly correlated across loop steps. Grouping channels of several loop steps into one sub-vector exploits this correlation and substantially reduces the reconstruction error at the same bitwidth, which makes the loop dimension an additional axis for vector quantization, complementary to the channel axis used by existing methods. We also find that quantization errors at different loop steps affect the model output to very different degrees. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, KV cache quantization method for looped models with two components. Loop-axis vector quantization codes channels of several loop steps jointly, so that one index is shared by multiple loop steps with no additional cost in bits. Loopaware codebook fine-tuning refines the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model, accounting for the unequal sensitivity of the loop steps. We evaluate LoopVQ on general benchmarks with Ouro1.4B, Ouro-2.6B (Zhu et al., 2025), and Huginn-3.5B (Geiping et al., 2026), and on long chain-of-thought reasoning and needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) tasks with the two Ouro models. Combined with TaSQ (Cheong et al., 2026b), which exploits structure along the channel axis, LoopVQ comes close to the BF16 baseline at 0.5 bit. We further implement LoopVQ in SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023), where the loop steps share the same indices and each reads them through its own slice of the codebook. Our contributions are as follows: We show that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. We propose LoopVQ, which combines loop-axis vector quantization with loop-aware codebook fine-tuning and is orthogonal to channel-axis methods such as TaSQ. At 0.5 and 0.25 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms vector quantization baselines designed for non-looped LLMs on general, reasoning, and long-context benchmarks. We implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where the quantized cache stores one index row for several loop steps. It nearly halves the decode latency at long contexts and increases the peak throughput by up to 4.3 and 6.1 on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

sections.title: 3 MOTIVATION
sections.content: Unlike the caches of different layers in non-looped model, the caches of layer in looped model are produced by applying the same parameters. We investigate whether this property can be used to compress the cache beyond what is achievable for non-looped model. Redundancy along the loop axis. The keys and values of layer are highly similar across loop steps, as they are computed by the same projection weights from hidden states of the same token (1). In Figure 2a, the keys of one head show nearly the same channel pattern at all four loop steps. Averaged over all layers and heads of Ouro-1.4B, the correlation between adjacent loop steps increases from 0.69 between the first two loop steps to 0.94 between the last two. This redundancy runs along different axis from the one that existing vector quantization methods exploit. Figure 2c measures how much this matters for quantization. At the same bitwidth and with the same number of codebooks, we only change which coordinates share code: channels of one loop step, or G/4 channels at each of four consecutive loop steps. With plain k-means, the second grouping roughly halves the reconstruction error of Ouro-1.4B at 0.5 bit, and reduces it substantially for both models at every bitwidth. Unequal quantization sensitivity across loop steps. Grouping along the loop axis places coordinates from different loop steps in one sub-vector, which is then encoded by single index. However, the loop steps do not affect the output equally. An error in the cache of an early loop step perturbs the hidden state passed to all later loop steps (1), whereas an error at the last loop step affects only that loop step. Table 1 confirms this. The sensitivity varies by roughly factor of five across loop steps: quantizing the first loop step is by far the most harmful, and the third loop step the least. The calibration objective (3) cannot express this difference within coupled sub-vector. Its weight ωn is single scalar per sub-vector, and its distance is the unweighted squared error, so an error is penalized equally regardless of the loop step on which it falls. The codebooks allocate the same precision to every loop step of sub-vector, although errors at some loop steps affect the output far more than errors at others. Existing KV cache quantization methods do not account for two properties of the looped structure: the cache is highly redundant along the loop axis, and the loop steps differ substantially in how strongly their quantization errors affect the output. Section 4 builds on both observations.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 Experimental setup Models. We evaluate Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B (Zhu et al., 2025) (Lb = 24 and 48, = 4, = 16, = 128), using their Thinking variants for reasoning tasks, and Huginn-3.5B (Geiping et al., 2026), which iterates fourlayer core block = 32 times between two-layer prelude and coda (132 KV caches per token, 55 heads of dimension 96). Methods. All methods quantize keys and values with 8bit codes (K = 256) and {16, 32}, i.e., 0.5 or 0.25 bits per element. The baselines are CQ (Zhang et al., 2024), with separate Fisher-weighted k-means codebook (3) per loop step and layer, and TaSQ (Cheong et al., 2026b), which transforms the keys before coding each loop step. LoopVQ couples Tc = 4 consecutive loop steps, so code spans = G/Tc channels (c = 4 at 0.5 bit, = 8 at 0.25 bit); on Huginn, the 32 loop steps form eight blocks, and the prelude and coda, which have no loop axis, are coded per layer as in CQ. TaSQ+LoopVQ applies TaSQs key transforms before coupling (Appendix B); its per-token key scale adds 0.008 bits per key element (0.003 on Huginn). Every method keeps the first and the most recent tokens in bf16: 8 and 64 on the general benchmarks, 64 and 256 on the reasoning and long-context benchmarks. Calibration. All codebooks are fitted separately for each model, including the Thinking variants, on 16 sequences of 2,048 tokens from the GPQA main set excluding the Diamond subset, which does not overlap with the evaluation set. sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Quantization of LLMs. Weight quantization methods for LLMs include scalar quantization with error compensation or activation-aware scaling (Frantar et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024), joint quantization of weights and activations (Xiao et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024), and vector quantization with codebooks (Tseng et al., 2024; Egiazarian et al., 2024). For the KV cache, scalar methods quantize keys and values per channel or per token (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024), and vector quantization methods code groups of channels jointly (Zhang et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2026b; Son et al., 2026). These methods target non-looped models, where each layer writes one cache, and quantize the caches of different layers independently. Quantization of looped transformers. The recurrence of looped transformers has motivated quantization methods tailored to it. LoopQ (Fang et al., 2026), LoopQuant (Zhao et al., 2026), and Loopy (Li et al., 2026) quantize the weights and activations of the shared block, accounting for the distribution shift and error accumulation across loop steps. For the KV cache, which dominates the memory of looped model (Figure 1a), FlashLoop (Yang & Liu, 2026) and ResidualQuant (Kim et al., 2026) apply scalar quantization at 2 to 4 bits per element. LoopVQ instead applies vector quantization along the loop axis to pretrained model, so that one index codes several loop steps, and compresses the KV cache below one bit per element.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented LoopVQ, KV cache quantization method for looped transformers. With BF16, attention grows with the context length and accounts for most of the decode time at 32K tokens, whereas with LoopVQ it stays below the time of the linear layers. At batch size 16, attention takes 1.87 ms per generated token with BF16 and 0.63 and 0.54 ms with LoopVQ at 0.5 and 0.25 bit. Encoding takes under 1% of the decode time and 5 to 7% of the prefill time. D.4 Reasoning stability across models and bitwidths Figure 16 extends Figure 10 to both Thinking models and both bitwidths. CQ and TaSQ exhaust the generation budget on large share of problems in every setting. TaSQ+LoopVQ follows the length distribution of BF16 in all four settings, and LoopVQ does so at 0.5 bit. Quantization errors can also end the reasoning early. With BF16, 16% and 22% of the generations of Ouro-1.4BThinking and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking end within 2K tokens. At 0.25 bit, this share rises to 33% and 59% with CQ and to 30% and 47% with TaSQ, whereas it stays at or below 30% with LoopVQ and TaSQ+LoopVQ in every setting.
